analysis.one_liner: Repeals about a dozen tax breaks and subsidies for oil and gas companies.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: it was referred to House Ways and Means on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal or limit about a dozen federal tax benefits enjoyed by the oil and gas industry, including credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, immediate deductions for drilling costs, percentage depletion, and LIFO accounting for the biggest oil companies [S2] [S3]. It would also apply the petroleum excise tax, which funds oil spill cleanup, to tar sands and oil shale oil [S3]. The result would be higher tax bills for oil companies and more federal revenue, paid for out of industry profits. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers generally, because the tax breaks the bill repeals would be worth billions in forgone revenue, and closing them would shift part of the federal tax burden off everyone else [S2]. Government treasuries would gain revenue from the oil and gas sector. Communities affected by oil spills would benefit modestly, because the bill extends the petroleum excise tax — which feeds the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund — to tar sands and oil shale oil [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals or trims a long list of oil and gas tax preferences — the marginal well credit, the enhanced oil recovery credit, immediate expensing of intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, the tertiary injectants deduction, and the passive-loss exception for oil and gas working interests — so producers pay closer to ordinary tax rates [S2] [S3].

Targets the largest companies directly: major integrated oil companies (roughly 500,000+ barrels of daily production and over $1 billion in gross receipts) would lose LIFO accounting, and foreign tax credits for payments to countries that give the company back an economic benefit would be limited [S2] [S3].

Expands the 'crude oil' definition for the federal petroleum excise tax to cover tar sands and oil shale oil, meaning those producers would start paying the tax that funds oil spill cleanup, and gives Treasury regulators authority to bring other new fuels into the tax as they emerge [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would pay higher federal taxes, and some of that could be passed along in slightly higher fuel prices. Small independent producers and operators of low-producing 'marginal' wells would be hit hardest, losing the credits and depletion deductions that help keep marginal wells running. Oil derived from tar sands and oil shale would face a new excise tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies, especially small producers

drawbacks.text: Higher taxes on producers can be passed through to consumers as somewhat higher fuel prices, so ordinary households would bear some of the cost at the pump [S2].

The repeal of the marginal well credit and percentage depletion would fall hardest on small, independent operators of low-output wells, whose elimination could shut down marginal wells sooner [S2] [S3].

The bill raises revenue for the general Treasury without dedicating it to anything — energy assistance, cleanup, or deficit reduction — so the public benefit is indirect rather than something households would see directly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but diffuse: closing industry tax preferences would raise significant revenue and level the playing field between oil and other energy investments, while the costs — a small pass-through to fuel prices and real pain for small marginal-well operators — are concentrated. An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill gives nothing specific back to the public and does not cushion small producers, and that a one-sided tax increase on an industry is exactly why it was never brought up.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on September 29, 2020 and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill with Rep. Sean Casten as cosponsor on September 29, 2020 [S1] [S3] [S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action of any kind was taken: the action history shows only the introduction and the committee referral, and the bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off because the bill died — they kept every tax break it would have repealed. The tax-writing committee also avoided a politically awkward vote on energy taxes during an election year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies that kept their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal oil and gas tax subsidies on September 29, 2020.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting the bill die at the end of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long lobbied Congress to preserve the tax provisions this bill would repeal, such as percentage depletion and intangible drilling cost expensing.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill's only sponsor and two cosponsors were all Democrats.

industries.note: The bill strips out the industry's core tax preferences — drilling cost expensing, percentage depletion, the marginal well and enhanced oil recovery credits, and more — raising its federal tax bill. Its gain in keeping them is forgone federal revenue that other taxpayers effectively cover.

The largest producers (500,000+ barrels per day, $1 billion+ in receipts) would lose LIFO accounting and face tighter foreign tax credit rules, raising their taxes further. These companies are the bill's most specific targets.
Producers of low-output wells depend on the marginal well credit and percentage depletion, both repealed by the bill. They are the industry segment with the most to lose.

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale producers
industries.note: Their products would be brought under the petroleum excise tax that funds oil spill cleanup for the first time, adding a per-barrel cost. They currently sell oil that escapes this levy.
